summary: Gyatsho Tshering (1936–2009) was a Tibetologist who studied at the University of Calcutta. He founded the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, serving as its Acting Director in 1972 and Director from 1974 to 1998.

Gyoei Fukuda (1867–1954) was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Tendai Daigakurin. He served as president of Taisho University (~1926–1944), a commissioned professor at the University of Tokyo (1928), and a lecturer at Toyo University.

Gyoei Takahashi (b. 1941) is a Buddhist studies scholar. Affiliations include Rissho University as assistant professor (attested 2003–2004) and professor (attested 2026), and the Institute for the Comprehensive Study of the Lotus Sutra as a member (attested 2004).

Gyoko Iotani (b. 1949), a Buddhist studies scholar, studied at Rissho University (~1968–1978). He served at Rissho University as assistant professor (~1983–1993), professor (~1993–2020), and professor emeritus (~2020), and at Minobusan University (attested 2026).

Gyokusen Hosaka (1887–1964) was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Komazawa University. He served as president of Komazawa Junior College from approximately 1950 to 1964 and taught Stanley Weinstein.
Gyomay Kubose (1905–2000) worked in Buddhist and religious studies. He studied at Otani University (~1937–1941) and was a student of Haya Akegarasu.
Gyoon Iotani is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Waseda University (attested 2015). By 2026, he held a post as deputy director at Minobusan University.
Gyosho Takahashi (b. 1949) is a Buddhist studies scholar. His academic posts include serving as professor at Minobusan Junior College (attested 1992) and Minobusan University (attested 1996).
Gyoshu Chojo is a Buddhist studies scholar who held posts as professor at Minobusan Junior College (attested 1996) and professor in the Faculty of Buddhism at Minobusan University (attested 2001).

Gyula Benigny (1890–1966) worked in linguistics and Indology, earning a Ph.D. from Eötvös Loránd University (~1908–1912). He taught at Debrecen Reformed Theological University (~1912–1919) and was a docent (1917) and extraordinary professor (1932–1949) at the University of Debrecen.
Gyula Ortutay (1910–1978) studied at the University of Szeged (1928–1934). He held a post at Nyugat and taught András Róna-Tas.
Gyula Wojtilla (b. 1945) is an Indologist. He studied under János Harmatta (~1963–1968), at Eötvös Loránd University (1964–1969), and at Banaras Hindu University (~1973–1974).

Gyurme Dorje (1950–2020) was a Tibetologist and Buddhist studies scholar who earned degrees from Edinburgh and SOAS. He held fellowships at SOAS/University of London (1991–1996) and was a translator for the Tsadra Foundation (2007–2020).
Gyurme Pema Tekchok studied under Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso.

György Hazai (1932–2016) worked in linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Eötvös Loránd University (~1949–1954) and held a post at the Institut für Orientforschung (~1970–1983).

György Kara (1935–2022) was a linguistics and Central Asian studies scholar who studied at ELTE, the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, and Saint Petersburg. He held posts at ELTE, directed at the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, and was professor at Indiana University Bloomington (1993–2022).

Gyōin Hashimoto (1897–1978) worked in Buddhist studies and philosophy, studying under Join Saeki and at the University of Tokyo (~1922–1925). He served as head priest of Yakushiji (1939–1967) and chief abbot of the Hosso School (1940).

Gábor Kovács is a Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar who earned an MA from Dharma Gate Buddhist College (2005–2010) and a PhD from Corvinus University of Budapest (2010–2017). He became an associate professor at Corvinus in 2018.
Gé Mang Khenchen Yönten Gyatso studied under Patrul Rinpoche and Jamgon Ju Mipham Gyatso, and taught Shechen Gyaltsab.

Gérard Barrigue de Fontainieu (1863–1927) was an Indologist who earned a diploma from the Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales by 1891. He was a pensionnaire at the École française d'Extrême-Orient (1901–1902).
